newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Albright demands trial for Bosnia war criminals.
newsitem.headline: Albright demands trial for Bosnia war criminals.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright travelled to the heart of Bosnian Serb territory Sunday to reassert American determination that indicted war criminals will be brought to justice.
In the northern town of Brcko, where Serb forces remain in control after seizing the area early in the Bosnian war, Albright warned that Washington wanted war crimes suspects to face trial.
"Brcko was the scene of some of the worst violence and brutality of the war," she said. "Make no mistake, a price will be paid for the atrocities that were committed here.
"Until it is paid by those who perpetrated the crimes, it will be paid by those who protected them."
Albright, hammering home her message with blunt language, toured the Balkans as part of a U.S. campaign to force compliance with the 1995 Dayton accords that ended the Bosnian conflict.
Her visit coincided with growing international concern that the fragile peace is unravelling, only a year before the NATO-led peace force is due to withdraw.
The U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague has indicted 75 people for war crimes, but most of them -- including former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic -- remain at large.

The United States has explored the possibility of a special military unit to snatch suspects and bring them to The Hague, but so far no action has been taken. Albright has said repeatedly that Washington is examining "all options."
After greeting U.S. peacekeeping troops stationed in Brcko, she flew to the north-western town of Banja Luka, where she met Biljana Plavsic, president of Bosnia's autonomous Serb republic.
By holding talks with Plavsic, Albright underscored Washington's position that it would work only with authorities who comply with the peace agreement.
The Banja Luka visit was seen as a rebuke to hardline allies of Karadzic in Pale, outside Sarajevo, who have tried to undercut Plavsic.
"The message here was that we respect Ms Plavsic. We think she is a responsible leader," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters afterward.

"We want to work with her and to associate, but we do need to see some action by the Bosnian Serb leadership to improve the situation. It is a message that really appeals to the self-interest of the Bosnian Serb population," he said.

Albright made clear in the meeting that substantial financial assistance was available to the Serbs if authorities allowed Moslem and Croat refugees to return to their homes, handed over indicted war criminals and upheld free movement for civilians as required by the Dayton treaty, Burns said.
Albright is the most senior U.S. official to visit the Bosnian Serb republic.
"We wanted to show symbolically that we're not trying to spurn the Serbs," Burns said. "Serbs have to be part of the future of Bosnia."
He said the tone of the meeting with Plavsic was constructive and, despite differences on most issues, "We heard a willingness to continue talking."
Ordinary Serbs, most of whom view Albright as a hostile enemy because of her outspoken comments during the war, were astounded that she had dared to step foot in Serb territory.

Albright could see about 200 protesters from her heavily armoured vehicle in Banja Luka. They carried placards cataloguing Serb complaints, including the fact that Croatia has been given membership in the Council of Europe and many Serbs are still missing from the war.
U.S. officials said Albright was trying to convey that Washington was at odds with the leadership but not with the Serb people.
Before her meeting with Albright, Plavsic critized the secretary for what she called her "anti-Serb statements" as U.N. ambassador.
As part of Washington's attempts to open a dialogue with the Bosnian Serbs, U.S. Special Envoy Robert Gelbard will revisit Banja Luka in mid-June.

During her stop in Brcko, Albright celebrated the reopening of a bridge that had been closed since war erupted in former Yugoslavia in 1991. She had urged Croatian President Franjo Tudjman Saturday to reopen the bridge, and he obliged.
Albright said that Brcko over the years had been an "open gate to the markets of Europe" and that opening the bridge would restore Bosnia's links to the rest of the continent.
In an appeal for tolerance, she said the bridge symbolised the "road to Europe."
"If you travel in that direction, you will eventually reach a Europe where borders unite rather than divide, a Europe where reason has triumphed over revenge..."
Balkan analysts said tough talk from Albright and Western powers needed to be followed through with action to break the iron grip of the nationalist parties dominating the country.
